Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
summary: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

title: Transcriptomic and Lipidomic Profiling of Human iPSC-Derived Microglia Reveals TREM2-Dependent and -Independent Processes
summary: TREM2 has been implicated in AD as a critical regulator of microglial functions and loss of function mutations in TREM2 increases one's risk of developing AD. Given the diverse functional roles of TREM2, we sought to unravel how it affects downstream pathways using human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs) derived from TREM2 knockout (KO) and isogenic control lines and assessing the response to oligomeric amyloid-{beta} 42 (oA{beta}42). While previous studies have primarily used fibrillar A{beta}, we focused on microglial responses to oA{beta}42 given their disease relevance and potent cytotoxic effects. At baseline, we identified a set of TREM2-dependent genes, which corresponded to the DAM signature in mice and disease-associated signatures in humans. Additionally, loss of TREM2 resulted in increased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes. In response to oA{beta}42, we found that the transcriptional response was largely TREM2-independent and corresponded to a strong induction of inflammatory pathways, with TREM2 also being downregulated in control iMGLs. We identified subsets of genes and pathways that were unique to either control, such as mitochondrial DNA and RNA degradation, or TREM2 KO iMGLs, such as the senescence-associated secretory pathway and adipogenesis, suggesting some differences in gene expression driven by TREM2 in response to oA{beta}42. Given that the inflammatory response was TREM2-independent, we sought to identify signaling pathways that contributed to inflammation. Inhibition of toll-like receptor signaling significantly reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory genes and modestly increased expression of TREM2 and TREM2-dependent genes. Consistent with our transcriptional data, cytokine production and secretion in response to oA{beta}42 was significantly increased to similar levels in both controls and TREM2 KO iMGLs. Lipidomic profiling of microglia revealed that triglycerides and lactosylceramides were significantly increased in both control and TREM2 KO iMGLs in response to oA{beta}42. TREM2 KO iMGLs had decreased levels of BMPs and increased levels of cholesterol esters across all conditions, further highlighting a role for TREM2 in maintaining lipid homeostasis in microglia. Taken together, we describe genes, pathways, and lipids that are associated with TREM2 expression that likely influence microglial responses to oA{beta}42.

title: Development of synthetic genetic arrays for studying interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes
summary: Mitochondria, the central axis of metabolism and energy transformation has emerged as a focal point for understanding the aging process and a plethora of human diseases. Yet, how the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes communicate is still unclear. This work aims to allow the analysis of such crosstalk by developing a genome-wide platform for studying genetic interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Using yeast as a model system in which mitochondrial homoplasmy and stable alterations in the mitochondrial genome can be generated by biolistic bombardment, we created a genome-wide library of yeast cells carrying nuclear deletions and temperature-sensitive mutations together with a superfolder-GFP reporter for the expression of the mitochondrial-encoded COX2 gene. Using this approach, we found links between nuclear-encoded processes and mitochondrial gene expression not previously anticipated, including a requirement for genes involved in MVB (multivesicular body) sorting/RIM signaling, vesicle trafficking/glycosylation, polarity, and peroxisome biogenesis, for maintaining mitochondrial COX2 expression. In contrast, defects in the autophagy machineries, ribosome biogenesis, and nuclear transcription and chromatin organization resulted in increased expression of COX2. While reduced COX2 expression correlated with a reduced expression of the nuclear-encoded TOM70 gene in mutants defect in mitochondrial functions, expression of the mitochondrial and nuclear genes responded differently to defects in cytoplasmic ribosome biogenesis and autophagy. When creating the COX2 expression library, we also found that cells devoid of mitochondrial DNA rely on the Rim101 signaling pathway, and many of its auxiliary regulatory factors, to maintain fitness. As mutations in the Rim101 signaling pathway also caused down-regulation of COX2 expression, it appears that Rim101 signaling is central for maintaining proper control of mitochondrial function. We believe the approach will allow for future genome-wide studies on how nuclear-encoded processes influence the translation, protein folding, and processing of mitochondria-encoded genes.

title: Coordinated remodeling of NAD⁺ metabolic networks across the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans
summary: Changes in the metabolic network that sustain NAD+ during aging remain poorly understood. Analysis of steady state levels is insufficient to reveal whether biosynthetic or consumption pathways are perturbed or preserved. Here, we address this gap in understanding by integrating metabolomics, proteomics, gene-expression profiling, and stable-isotope tracing across the Caenorhabditis elegans adult lifespan. NAD abundance increases with age despite reductions in selected biosynthetic components. Tracing reveals reduced mid-adult incorporation of nicotinamide and nicotinic acid into NAD, alongside declining nicotinamide riboside abundance and loss of detectable nicotinic acid-derived labeling into this precursor. Early mitochondrial Complex I remodeling accompanies sustained changes in redox and energetic indices. Disruption of NAD-consuming or salvage enzymes reduces reproduction and lifespan, whereas precursor supplementation provides no longevity benefit under the conditions tested. Together, these findings reveal that NAD accumulation can coexist with extensive metabolic remodeling, establishing the importance of evaluating network dynamics beyond cofactor abundance.

title: Combined nelfinavir and cisplatin treatment promotes inflammatory signaling and immunogenic cell death in ovarian cancer cells
summary: Platinum (Pt) based chemotherapy remains central to ovarian cancer (OC) treatment, but recurrent disease frequently develops Pt resistance and responds poorly to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Immunogenic cell death (ICD) links tumor cell killing to antitumor immunity; however, cisplatin (CDDP), widely used in OC, is an incomplete ICD inducer. We previously demonstrated that the HIV protease inhibitor nelfinavir (NFV) enhances CDDP induced OC cell death and promotes a lytic, pyroptosis associated phenotype. Here, we investigated whether NFV enhances the immunogenic consequences of CDDP treatment. RNA seq analysis of OC cells treated with CDDP, NFV, or their combination revealed enrichment of interferon (IFN) associated, cytoplasmic DNA sensing, inflammatory chemokine, and antigen presentation pathways following NFV containing treatments. NFV alone and CDDP plus NFV reduced mature Lamin A abundance and increased extranuclear double stranded DNA accumulation. Cytosolic fractionation and droplet digital PCR demonstrated increased cytosolic TP53 DNA, particularly following combined treatment. CDDP plus NFV increased STING and TBK1 phosphorylation, supporting engagement of the cGAS STING TBK1 signaling pathway. The combination enhanced release of inflammatory and ICD associated mediators, including HMGB1, IL18, and IFNbeta. Importantly, vaccination with CDDP plus NFV-treated murine ID8 OC cells protected immunocompetent female mice against subsequent live ID8 cell challenge, reducing tumor incidence and burden. In contrast, ID8 cells killed by freeze thaw-induced accidental necrosis provided no comparable protection. Collectively, these findings indicate that NFV enhances the immunogenic consequences of CDDP induced OC cell death, potentially involving cytoplasmic DNA accumulation and STING TBK1 signaling, and promotes protective antitumor immunity in vivo. These results support further investigation of NFV as a repurposed partner for Pt based chemotherapy and its potential combination with immunotherapy in OC.

title: CD38-NAMPT-p21 signaling promotes stress adaptation in CLL
summary: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is the most common adult leukemia in the United States, accounting for ~30% of new diagnoses and ~4,000 deaths annually. High CD38 expression is a well-established marker of poor prognosis, yet the mechanistic basis of CD38-mediated treatment failure has remained incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that CD38 functions not merely as a prognostic biomarker but as a metabolic and signaling regulator that equips CLL cells to withstand cytotoxic and hypoxic stress. Using MEC-1 cells engineered to express CD38, we identified a CD38-NAMPT-p21 survival axis that confers resistance to fludarabine and hypoxia. CD38 NADase activity promoted NAMPT upregulation and AKT activation and was associated with accumulation of cytoplasmic p21. This CD38-dependent phenotype was lost in cells expressing a catalytically inactive CD38 mutant and was also reversed by pharmacologic inhibition of NAMPT (FK866) or suppression of p21 (UC2288). Analysis of three independent single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets of primary CLL further showed that naturally occurring CD38-positive CLL cells exhibit increased NAMPT expression and related stress-response signaling. Analysis of larger primary CLL cohorts further linked NAMPT expression to AKT and hypoxia signatures, providing additional support for the relevance of this pathway in patient-derived CLL. Together, these findings identify CD38-NAMPT-p21 signaling as an important mechanism of stress adaptation in CLL and suggest that targeting NAD metabolism and p21-mediated survival pathways may represent a potential strategy for CD38-high disease.

title: Integrating redox dynamics and gene networks reveals ROS-mediated control of Arabidopsis seed germination under water stress
summary: Seed germination is a critical step of plant development that is highly sensitive to water availability. During this delicate transition, water stress responses are tightly regulated by multilevel molecular networks that integrate environmental cues into developmental adaptations. Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) play a positive signaling role in seed germination, yet their influence on germination under water stress remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the involvement of ROS in Arabidopsis thaliana seed germination upon reproducibly reducing water potential using polyethylene glycol (PEG). The data show that delayed germination under water stress is not simply a consequence of reduced water uptake. Instead, water stress triggers coordinated reprogramming events characterized by altered H2O2 homeostasis, particularly in peroxisomes, which functionally mediates a rebalancing of ABA and GA metabolism toward developmental slowdown. A weighted gene co-expression network analysis of water-stress transcriptomic dynamics identified a gene hub associated with H2O2 production during germination, shedding light on multiple oxygen- and redox-related processes that are strongly linked to transcriptional and translational attenuation. Collectively, this study unveils a role for regulating peroxisomal H2O2 homeostasis in Arabidopsis seed water stress responses, offering new perspectives for improving crop resilience to environmental constraints.
